ann_85.text: Through this part, an international plan clearly raises the typical customer's predicted chance of leaving from about 1% to about 20%.

Customer-service calls slightly raise it steadily, each extra call adding about the same, from about 1% at 0 calls to about 4% at 3 calls, and a higher night-time charge slightly raises it steadily to about 2%.

More daytime minutes slightly lower it steadily, from about 2% at 112 minutes to about 1% at 249 minutes, more evening minutes slightly lower it steadily and a voice-mail plan slightly lowers it, and more international minutes, a higher evening charge and a longer account slightly raise it steadily, while more night-time minutes (in an uneven way) and area code 510 slightly raise it (on the training data only).

California slightly raises it to about 5%, Washington to about 4%, Montana to about 3% and Massachusetts, Louisiana, New York, Maryland, Minnesota, Kentucky, Arizona and Oregon to about 1% to 2%, while Hawaii, New Jersey, Vermont and Illinois slightly lower it to below 1% and nine other states to about 1% (on the training data only).

ann_86.text: Through this part, customer-service calls slightly add to the predicted chance of leaving from 4 calls upwards, in an uneven way: for the typical customer, going from 0 to 4 calls moves it from about 1% to about 3%.

For a typical customer with 3 customer-service calls (one in Idaho), a daytime charge above about 26.35 US dollars slightly lowers it in an uneven way, from about 5% to about 3%, and a higher evening charge lowers it only slightly, barely moving it (on the training data only).
Being in Alaska or Ohio slightly raises it and being in Iowa or Texas slightly lowers it, all staying at about 1% (on the training data only).

ann_87.text: Through this part, a higher daytime charge clearly raises the predicted chance of leaving: nothing until about 32.38 US dollars, where this part switches on, then steadily; for the typical customer, going from 0 to 46.09 US dollars moves it from about 1% to about 33%.

Over the usual range it clearly raises it the same way (nothing until about that point, then steadily), from about 1% at 19.07 US dollars to about 17% at 42.40 US dollars, but only if the customer has no voice-mail messages, and then in an uneven way across customers; customers with some stay at about 1%.
This part acts on 1390 of 4000 customers, 305 of whom left; for the typical one (a customer in Alabama with about 219 daytime minutes) it slightly raises the chance from below 1% to about 3%.
For a typical customer in Alabama with about 218 daytime minutes, voice-mail messages slightly lower it in an uneven way, only while they stay below about 8 messages, from about 3% to below 1%.
Customer-service calls (0 to 3) slightly lower it through this part, in an uneven way (on the training data only).

ann_88.text: This part acts on 1030 of 4000 customers, 288 of whom left, and clearly raises the typical one's predicted chance of leaving (a customer in Alabama with about 234 daytime and 236 evening minutes) from about 4% to about 13%.
More daytime minutes slightly raise it: nothing until about 222 minutes, where this part switches on, then steadily; for the typical customer, from about 1% to about 6%.
A higher evening charge slightly raises it, slowly at first, then faster, and even more so for customers with over 180 daytime minutes: from about 1% to about 4%, against about 1% to about 2%.

Across the usual range, the daytime-minutes rise (nothing until about that point, then steadily) slightly moves it from about 1% to about 3%, and a higher evening charge slightly raises it in an uneven way, from about 1% to about 2%.
For the typical customer this part acts on, being in North Carolina slightly lowers it from about 13% to about 9%, and being in Maryland slightly raises it to about 15% (on the training data only).

For a typical customer in New Hampshire, the evening charge slightly adds to it only once it rises above about 21.83 US dollars, in an uneven way, from about 2% to about 4% (the model has little data on this: 13 customers there are past that point).

ann_89.text: Through this part, a higher daytime charge slightly lowers the predicted chance of leaving once it rises above about 23.13 US dollars, in an uneven way, from about 2% to about 1% for the typical customer (on the training data only).
This part acts on 3149 of 4000 customers, 454 of whom left; for the typical one (with about 194 daytime minutes) it slightly lowers the chance from about 3% to about 2% (on the training data only).
Being in Alaska slightly lowers it to below 1% and being in New Hampshire slightly raises it to about 2% (on the training data only).

ann_90.text: Through this part, customer-service calls (0 to 3) slightly lower the predicted chance of leaving in an uneven way, from about 2% to about 1% (on the training data only).

ann_91.text: Through this part, being in New Jersey raises the typical customer's predicted chance of leaving from about 1% to about 14% (on the training data only).
Through the main part of the model, New Jersey instead slightly lowers it to below 1%, and across the whole model it slightly raises it to about 3% (on the training data only).
South Carolina and Indiana slightly raise it to about 2%, while Vermont and Wyoming slightly lower it to about 1% or below (on the training data only).

ann_92.text: Across the whole model, an international plan clearly raises the typical customer's predicted chance of leaving from about 1% to about 20%.

Being in California rather than one of the states the model does not single out slightly raises it to about 5%, Washington to about 4%, Montana and New Jersey to about 3% and eleven other states to about 1% to 2%, while Vermont, Hawaii, Alaska and Illinois slightly lower it to below 1% and eleven other states to about 1% (on the training data only).

A higher evening charge slightly raises it in an uneven way and a higher night-time charge slightly raises it steadily, both to about 2%, and more voice-mail messages slightly lower it in an uneven way, staying at about 1%.
More international minutes slightly raise it steadily, from about 1% at 7 minutes to about 2% at 14 minutes (on the training data only).

A longer account slightly raises it steadily, more night-time minutes slightly raise it in an uneven way and area code 510 slightly raises it, while more evening minutes slightly lower it steadily and a voice-mail plan slightly lowers it, all staying at about 1% (on the training data only).
